etymology: A compound of before and time, used adverbially. Webster 1828: formerly; of old time. The Authorized Version uses it to mark what a thing used to be, usually where the change is the point of the sentence.
biblical_def: Beforetime marks what used to be, and Scripture uses it at hinges where something has changed for good. Its most valuable use is a parenthesis explaining an obsolete word to a later generation: Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer (1 Samuel 9:9). The inspired writer pauses to gloss his own vocabulary, which is a small but real witness to the care with which Scripture was transmitted. It marks a city’s former standing at the moment of its fall: Joshua at that time turned back, and took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword: for Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms (Joshua 11:10). It marks what a man used to do before the gospel came to his city: there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one (Acts 8:9). And it marks a reputation that made a new thing astonishing: when all that knew him beforetime saw that, behold, he prophesied among the prophets… Is Saul also among the prophets? (1 Samuel 10:11).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BEFORETIME as formerly; of old time; in time past — a compound adverb now largely obsolete except in the Scriptures.
webster_full: BEFORETIME, adv. — Formerly; of old time; in time past.
Used to mark a former state or practice which has since been altered.
Compounded of before, in front or previous to, and time.
Now nearly obsolete in common English, but retained in the Authorized Version.
Compare the parallel compounds heretofore, hitherto, and aforetime.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 9:9
(Beforetime in Israel, when a man went to enquire of God, thus he spake, Come, and let us go to the seer: for he that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer.)
Joshua 11:10
And Joshua at that time turned back, and took Hazor, and smote the king thereof with the sword: for Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms.
Acts 8:9
But there was a certain man, called Simon, which beforetime in the same city used sorcery, and bewitched the people of Samaria, giving out that himself was some great one:
1 Samuel 10:11

And it came to pass, when all that knew him beforetime saw that, behold, he prophesied among the prophets, then the people said one to another, What is this that is come unto the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?
corruption_summary: Simon of Samaria is the Bible’s case of a man who believed, was baptized, and continued to think of divine power as something purchasable, and the church has treated his name as a category ever since without much noticing how many of his instincts it has adopted.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 8 says Simon beforetime used sorcery and gave out that he was some great one, and that the people from the least to the greatest called him the great power of God. Then Philip preached, and Simon believed also: and when he was baptized, he continued with Philip. When he saw the Spirit given through the apostles’ hands he offered money for the ability, and Peter answered, Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money… thy heart is not right in the sight of God. The old trade had changed its vocabulary and kept its logic: power to be acquired, displayed, and monetised. That is worth applying honestly to any ministry organised around the transfer of anointing for a price, and it is also the origin of the word simony.

1 Samuel 9:9 is a smaller but genuinely useful text, because it shows Scripture explaining itself across a change in usage. The writer knows his readers no longer say seer, so he tells them what it meant. That is a model for how the church should handle its own vocabulary: not by abandoning the older word, which carries something the newer one has lost, but by explaining it. The whole enterprise of this dictionary rests on the same conviction, and 1 Samuel 9:9 is its warrant — an inspired gloss, placed in parentheses, so that a later generation would not lose the sense.
roots_summary: Hebrew lephanim (H6440 with preposition), formerly, in former times; ethmol (H865), yesterday, formerly; Greek proteron (G4386), before, formerly; prouparcho (G4391), to exist previously.
roots_lines: Hebrew lephanim — literally to the face, and so before, formerly; the beforetime of 1 Samuel 9:9 and Joshua 11:10.
Hebrew ethmol (H865) — yesterday, in time past; often joined with shilshom, the day before, for the idiom of former days.
Greek proteron (G4386) — formerly, before; ye know how through infirmity of the flesh I preached the gospel unto you at the first (Galatians 4:13).
Greek prouparcho (G4391) — to be before, to exist previously; Simon, which beforetime… used sorcery (Acts 8:9).
Hebrew roeh (H7203) — a seer; the older title glossed as prophet in 1 Samuel 9:9.
usage: He that is now called a Prophet was beforetime called a Seer (1 Samuel 9:9) — Scripture glossing its own older vocabulary.
Hazor beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms (Joshua 11:10) — a former standing named at the moment of its fall.
Simon, which beforetime… used sorcery (Acts 8:9) — the old trade with a new vocabulary and the same logic.

etymology: From all and ready, run together. Webster 1828: before or by this time; at this present time or a specified time. In the New Testament it carries a heavy doctrinal load — the unbeliever condemned already, the mystery of iniquity working already, the harvest white already.
biblical_def: Already in the New Testament repeatedly says that a thing supposed to be future is present. Of the unbeliever’s standing: He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God (John 3:18). The condemnation is not a sentence awaiting the last day but a verdict already in force; the judgment day will publish it, not create it. Of evil in the world: For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way (2 Thessalonians 2:7) — written in the first century, of a lawlessness already operating under restraint. Of the harvest: Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest (John 4:35), said in Samaria as the townspeople were coming out to Him. And of Christian attainment, in the great denial that keeps the doctrine of sanctification honest: Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus (Philippians 3:12).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ALREADY as before or by this time; at this present time or a specified time; noting that the thing spoken of has taken place sooner than might have been expected.
webster_full: ALREADY, adv. — Before or by this time; at the present time or a time specified.
Noting that a thing has taken place sooner than expected, or before the time in question.
Compounded of all and ready, that is, wholly ready or wholly done.
In Scripture, often used to bring a supposed future condition into the present.
Compare alway, altogether, and other compounds of all in the Authorized Version.
scriptures: John 3:18
He that believeth on him is not condemned: but he that believeth not is condemned already, because he hath not believed in the name of the only begotten Son of God.
2 Thessalonians 2:7
For the mystery of iniquity doth already work: only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way.
John 4:35
Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest.
Philippians 3:12
Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: John 3:18 says the unbeliever is condemned already, which contradicts the widespread assumption that people are neutral before God until some future assessment, and Philippians 3:12 forbids the opposite error of claiming attained perfection.
corruption_paragraphs: The default religious picture has humanity in a neutral condition, waiting for a verdict that will be rendered later on the balance of a life. John 3:18 denies it in the plainest terms: the unbeliever is condemned already, and the stated ground is that he has not believed on the name of the only begotten Son of God. This is the necessary background to John 3:16; a rescue implies present danger. It also explains why the New Testament’s evangelism has urgency in it and modern evangelism often does not. Nobody hurries to warn a man in a neutral condition. Paul’s summary in Ephesians 2:3 is the same doctrine in different words: we were by nature the children of wrath, even as others — by nature, not by verdict pending.

Philippians 3:12 guards the other flank, and it is worth quoting against every perfectionist scheme. Paul — converted on the Damascus road, caught up to the third heaven, author of most of the New Testament epistles — says flatly that he has not already attained and is not already perfect. He describes himself as pressing toward the mark, forgetting the things behind, reaching forth. If Paul at the end of his ministry disclaims perfection, the entire-sanctification and second-blessing traditions are claiming for ordinary believers what the apostle would not claim for himself. And 2 Thessalonians 2:7 completes the picture of the age in which both truths must be held: the mystery of iniquity is already at work, restrained but present, so the believer lives between a condemnation escaped and a perfection not yet reached.
roots_summary: Greek ede (G2235), already, now; krino (G2919), to judge; teleioo (G5048), to complete, to make perfect; Hebrew kebar (H3528), already, long since.
roots_lines: Greek ede (G2235) — already, by this time; condemned already (John 3:18) and white already to harvest (John 4:35).
Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, to condemn; the perfect tense in John 3:18 marks a standing verdict.
Greek teleioo (G5048) — to complete, to bring to the goal; were already perfect (Philippians 3:12).
Greek mysterion (G3466) — a mystery, something once hidden now disclosed; the mystery of iniquity (2 Thessalonians 2:7).
Hebrew kebar (H3528) — already, long ago; a favourite word of Ecclesiastes (Ecclesiastes 1:10).
usage: He that believeth not is condemned already (John 3:18) — a verdict in force, not a sentence pending.
The mystery of iniquity doth already work (2 Thessalonians 2:7) — lawlessness present, and restrained.
Not as though I had already attained (Philippians 3:12) — the apostle disclaiming what perfectionism claims.

etymology: A compound of here and after. Webster 1828: in time to come; in a future state. In the Gospels it is repeatedly the Lord’s word for what His disciples and His judges will see later, and in Revelation it divides the book.
biblical_def: Hereafter in the Gospels is the Lord’s word for a sight or a knowledge deferred. To Nathanael, after one sentence of insight had convinced him: Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man (John 1:51) — the ladder of Jacob’s dream identified as a Person. To Peter, resisting the towel and basin: What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter (John 13:7), which is the pattern of most providences and nearly all of them that hurt. To the high priest at His trial, under oath, in the most dangerous sentence He ever spoke: Thou hast said: nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven (Matthew 26:64) — the accused telling the court that it will next see Him as its Judge. And Revelation uses the word to divide John’s commission: Write the things which thou hast seen, and the things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter (Revelation 1:19).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HEREAFTER as in time to come; in some future time or state; and, as a noun, a future state or the time to come after the present life.
webster_full: HEREAFTER, adv. — In time to come; in some future time or state.
HEREAFTER, n. — A future state; the time or condition that succeeds the present life.
Compounded of here and after; literally, after this.
In Scripture, used both of a near future within the speaker’s lifetime and of the world to come.
Compare the parallel compounds hereby, herein, hereof, and hereunto.
scriptures: John 1:51
And he saith unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.
John 13:7
Jesus answered and said unto him, What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter.
Matthew 26:64
Jesus saith unto him, Thou hast said: nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven.
Revelation 1:19
Write the things which thou hast seen, and the things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter;
corruption_summary: John 13:7 promises understanding later and not now, which the modern insistence on immediate explanation for every hard providence refuses to accept, and the answer offered instead is usually a reason God has not given.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter’s objection was reasonable by every ordinary standard: his Master should not be washing his feet. The Lord’s answer grants that he does not understand and does not explain — What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter. That is the standing shape of God’s dealings, and it is the answer Job received out of the whirlwind, where the reader has been told about the heavenly court in chapter one and Job never is. Against this, the modern comforter is expected to supply a reason, and supplies one: God needed another angel, everything happens for a purpose, He is teaching you something specific. Almost all of it is invented, and Job’s friends were rebuked for exactly that. The honest word is the Lord’s own: not now, hereafter.

Matthew 26:64 sets the boldest use in the most dangerous setting. Caiaphas puts Jesus under oath to say whether He is the Christ, the Son of God, and the answer is Thou hast said — followed by a claim built from Daniel 7 and Psalm 110: the court will see the accused seated at the right hand of power and coming in the clouds. The high priest tore his clothes and called it blasphemy, which was the correct response if the claim was false. There is no third option available. Revelation 1:19 completes the pattern by making the deferred sight the subject of a book: what John has seen, what is, and what shall be hereafter — given so that the church would know the end before it arrived.
roots_summary: Greek ap arti, from now on; meta tauta (G3326 with G5023), after these things; mello (G3195), to be about to; Hebrew acharith (H319), the latter end.
roots_lines: Greek ap arti — from this moment onward; the hereafter of John 1:51 and Matthew 26:64.
Greek meta tauta — after these things; the hereafter of Revelation 1:19, and the phrase that opens Revelation 4:1.
Greek mello (G3195) — to be about to happen; the verb of things shortly to come to pass.
Hebrew acharith (H319) — the after part, the latter end; the latter end of that man (Job 42:12).
Greek arti (G737) — now, at this moment; thou knowest not now (John 13:7).
usage: Hereafter ye shall see heaven open (John 1:51) — Jacob’s ladder identified as a Person.
Thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter (John 13:7) — the standing shape of hard providences.
Hereafter shall ye see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power (Matthew 26:64) — the accused naming the court’s next sight of Him.

etymology: A compound of even (evening) and tide in its old sense of time or season, as in Yuletide and noontide. Webster 1828: the time of evening. The Authorized Version also uses the sister form eveningtide.
biblical_def: Eventide is the Authorized Version’s word for the close of the day, and Scripture places some of its weightiest moments there. Mark ends the triumphal entry not with a celebration but with an inspection and a departure: And Jesus entered into Jerusalem, and into the temple: and when he had looked round about upon all things, and now the eventide was come, he went out unto Bethany with the twelve (Mark 11:11). He looks at everything, says nothing, and leaves; the cleansing comes the next morning. Luke marks the first arrest of the apostles by the hour: they laid hands on them, and put them in hold unto the next day: for it was now eventide (Acts 4:3) — a night in custody because the courts had closed. Isaiah uses the sister form eveningtide for the suddenness with which an enemy is dealt with: And behold at eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us (Isaiah 17:14). Trouble at dusk and the trouble gone by dawn — the reversal accomplished in the dark, while the people it protects are asleep.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives EVENTIDE as the time of evening; the evening season. It is compounded of even, the close of day, and tide, which in old English signified time or season rather than the movement of the sea.
webster_full: EVENTIDE, n. — The time of evening; the evening season.
EVEN, n. — The close of the day; the latter part or decline of the day.
TIDE, n. — In its old and primary sense, time or season, as in Yuletide, noontide, and Whitsuntide.
The Authorized Version also uses the sister form EVENINGTIDE with the same meaning.
From Saxon aefen, evening, and tid, time — the root also of tidings in the sense of what is timely.
scriptures: Mark 11:11
And Jesus entered into Jerusalem, and into the temple: and when he had looked round about upon all things, and now the eventide was come, he went out unto Bethany with the twelve.
Acts 4:3
And they laid hands on them, and put them in hold unto the next day: for it was now eventide.
Isaiah 17:14
And behold at eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us.
Psalm 22:2
O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent.
corruption_summary: Mark 11:11 shows Christ surveying the temple in silence at eventide and acting the following morning, which is a deliberate and instructive contrast to the modern habit of immediate public reaction to whatever has just been seen.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark alone records the pause. Matthew compresses the entry and the cleansing into one day; Mark says the Lord came in, looked round about upon all things, saw that it was late, and went out to Bethany. The cleansing happens the next morning, after a night, and after the cursing of the fig tree that frames it. Whatever else this teaches, it does not teach impulsiveness. Righteous anger in Scripture is deliberate: God is slow to anger, and James says let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath. The contemporary reflex — to see, to react, and to publish within the hour — would have produced a different scene in the temple and a worse one. A night between the seeing and the acting is not weakness.

Isaiah 17:14 supplies the promise attached to the hour. At eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not. The Assyrian host that terrified Jerusalem was dealt with in a single night (Isaiah 37:36), and the verse generalises it: this is the portion of them that spoil us. God works in the dark, while the people He is protecting are asleep and can do nothing. Psalm 22:2 is placed here as the honest counterweight, because Scripture also records the nights when nothing appears to happen: O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent — words the Lord Jesus took to Himself on the cross, and the psalm ends in triumph anyway.
roots_summary: Hebrew ereb (H6153), evening; eth ereb, the time of evening; Greek hespera (G2073), evening; opsios (G3798), late, evening.
roots_lines: Hebrew ereb (H6153) — evening; the second half of the biblical day, which begins at sunset (Genesis 1:5).
Hebrew eth ereb — the time of evening; behind eveningtide in Isaiah 17:14.
Greek hespera (G2073) — evening; it was now eventide (Acts 4:3), and abide with us: for it is toward evening (Luke 24:29).
Greek opsios (G3798) — late, the evening hour; now the eventide was come (Mark 11:11).
Hebrew bin haarbayim — between the evenings; the appointed time for the passover lamb (Exodus 12:6).
usage: Now the eventide was come, he went out unto Bethany (Mark 11:11) — a survey in silence, and the action deferred to morning.
It was now eventide (Acts 4:3) — a night in custody because the courts had closed.
At eveningtide trouble; and before the morning he is not (Isaiah 17:14) — the reversal accomplished in the dark.

etymology: A compound of day and time. Webster 1828: the time of daylight; the period between sunrise and sunset. Scripture uses it to mark unanswered prayer, the shade God provides, the Lord’s public teaching, and the shamelessness of open sin.
biblical_def: Daytime in Scripture usually stands opposite night in a pair, and the pairing carries the meaning. The psalm of the cross opens with it: O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent (Psalm 22:2) — round the clock, and no answer, which is the psalm the Lord Jesus quoted from the cross. Isaiah promises a canopy over the restored Zion: there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain (Isaiah 4:6), which reaches back to the pillar of cloud and forward to Revelation 7:15. Luke describes the rhythm of the Lord’s last week with the same contrast: in the day time he was teaching in the temple; and at night he went out, and abode in the mount that is called the mount of Olives (Luke 21:37) — public teaching by day, and nights outdoors, in the week He was to be killed. And Peter marks the effrontery of false teachers by the hour of their indulgence: as they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time (2 Peter 2:13), the point being that even the world reserves such conduct for the dark.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives DAYTIME as the time of daylight; the period from sunrise to sunset, as distinguished from the night.
webster_full: DAYTIME, n. — The time of daylight; the period between the rising and the setting of the sun.
Opposed to night, and often set against it in Scripture to signify the whole of a duration.
Used figuratively of a season of light, opportunity, or open conduct.
DAY, n. — That part of the time of the earth’s revolution on its axis in which its surface is presented to the sun.
Compounded of Saxon daeg, day, and tima, time.
scriptures: Psalm 22:2
O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent.
Isaiah 4:6
And there shall be a tabernacle for a shadow in the daytime from the heat, and for a place of refuge, and for a covert from storm and from rain.
Luke 21:37
And in the day time he was teaching in the temple; and at night he went out, and abode in the mount that is called the mount of Olives.
2 Peter 2:13

And shall receive the reward of unrighteousness, as they that count it pleasure to riot in the day time. Spots they are and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you;
corruption_summary: Psalm 22:2 records God not hearing, and the modern devotional habit of assuring every sufferer that God is answering in some invisible way declines to say what the psalm itself says.
corruption_paragraphs: The psalm begins My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? and continues I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not. It is in the canon in that form, and the Lord Jesus took its opening line onto the cross, where the forsaking was real and not merely felt. Scripture therefore gives believers permission to say the hardest thing about their own experience, in prayer, to God. What it does not give is permission to stop there: the same psalm turns at verse 22 and ends with all the ends of the world remembering and turning unto the LORD. The dictionary’s position is that a piety which cannot voice verse 2 will not be able to hold on to verse 31, because a faith that must first be edited to be spoken is not being exercised at all.

2 Peter 2:13 supplies a sharper and more topical use. The false teachers Peter describes count it pleasure to riot in the day time, and the phrase assumes a shared standard: even a pagan society kept such things for the night. Romans 13:13 makes the same appeal — let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness. What is new in our own moment is not the conduct but the daylight; the shame that once drove sin into the dark has largely gone, and it is now performed, published, and defended. Peter’s word for such men is spots… and blemishes, and he places them not outside the church but feasting with it.
roots_summary: Hebrew yomam (H3119), by day, daily; yom (H3117), day; Greek hemera (G2250), day; en hemera, in the daytime.
roots_lines: Hebrew yomam (H3119) — by day, in the daytime; I cry in the daytime (Psalm 22:2).
Hebrew yom (H3117) — day; the root, and the word of the six days of creation.
Greek hemera (G2250) — day; in the day time he was teaching in the temple (Luke 21:37).
Hebrew lailah (H3915) — night; the constant counterpart in these pairings.
Hebrew tsel (H6738) — a shadow, shade; a shadow in the daytime from the heat (Isaiah 4:6).
usage: I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not (Psalm 22:2) — the hardest thing a believer can say, said in prayer.
A shadow in the daytime from the heat (Isaiah 4:6) — the pillar of cloud promised again over Zion.
They that count it pleasure to riot in the day time (2 Peter 2:13) — sin that no longer needs the dark.

etymology: From Saxon gestran daeg, the day before this. Webster 1828: the day last past; the day next before the present. Scripture uses it for the brevity of man’s knowledge, the brevity of a thousand years before God, and the unchangeableness of Christ.
biblical_def: Yesterday is one of Scripture’s measuring words, and it is used to measure three different things. It measures how little men know: For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow (Job 8:9) — spoken by Bildad, and true in itself even though he applied it wrongly. It measures a millennium from God’s side: For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night (Psalm 90:4), in the psalm of Moses, the oldest in the Psalter, which sets God’s eternity against a lifespan of seventy years and asks Him to teach us to number our days. Peter quotes the same measure to answer scoffers about the delay of the second coming. And most importantly it measures Christ, who is not measured by it at all: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever (Hebrews 13:8). The verse sits between a command to remember dead leaders and a warning against strange doctrines, which is exactly where it is needed: teachers pass, teachings shift, and the Object of faith does not.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines YESTERDAY as the day last past; the day next before the present; and figuratively, a short time past or lately.
webster_full: YESTERDAY, n. — The day last past; the day next before the present.
As an adverb, on the day last past; as, he came yesterday.
Figuratively, a very short time past; recently; as, we are but of yesterday.
In Scripture, used to express both the brevity of human life and the shortness of long ages before God.
From Saxon gestran, yester, and daeg, day — the root of yesteryear and yestereve.
scriptures: Hebrews 13:8
Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
Psalm 90:4
For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night.
Job 8:9
(For we are but of yesterday, and know nothing, because our days upon earth are a shadow:)
Isaiah 35:10
And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
corruption_summary: Hebrews 13:8 is quoted constantly to guarantee that whatever God did in a past revival or in an apostle’s ministry He is obliged to repeat, when the verse is about the immutability of Christ’s Person and is set as a guard against novel doctrines.
corruption_paragraphs: The context governs the meaning and it is usually skipped. Verse 7 says Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation. Verse 8 says Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, to day, and for ever. Verse 9 says Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. The leaders die; the Christ they preached does not change; therefore do not go chasing novelties. The verse is a doctrinal anchor, not a warrant for expecting particular phenomena. Used the popular way it proves far too much: God has not repeated the plagues of Egypt, the crossing of the sea, or the giving of the law, and no one supposes His immutability requires Him to.

Psalm 90:4 corrects a different distortion. Peter applies it directly to those who mock the delay of Christ’s return: one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward (2 Peter 3:8-9). The apparent delay is not indifference and it is not incapacity; it is patience with a purpose, and the purpose is that men should come to repentance. Job 8:9 supplies the posture that follows from both verses. We are of yesterday and know nothing — which was Bildad’s truest sentence, and he ruined it by using it to accuse a righteous man.
roots_summary: Hebrew ethmol (H865), yesterday; temol (H8543), yesterday, formerly; Greek chthes (G5504), yesterday; echthes, the same.
roots_lines: Hebrew ethmol (H865) — yesterday, in time past; we are but of yesterday (Job 8:9).
Hebrew temol (H8543) — yesterday; often paired with shilshom for the idiom in time past.
Greek chthes (G5504) — yesterday; Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever (Hebrews 13:8).
Greek ho autos — the same; the emphatic phrase of Hebrews 13:8, also used of God in Hebrews 1:12.
Hebrew ashmurah (H821) — a night watch; as a watch in the night (Psalm 90:4).
usage: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever (Hebrews 13:8) — set between dying leaders and strange doctrines.
A thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday (Psalm 90:4) — the measure Peter applies to the delay of the coming.
We are but of yesterday, and know nothing (Job 8:9) — Bildad’s truest sentence, wrongly applied.

etymology: A compound of often and times. Webster 1828: frequently; often; many times. The Authorized Version also uses the shorter ofttimes. Its most weighty use is in Hebrews, where the repetition of a sacrifice proves its insufficiency.
biblical_def: Oftentimes means repeatedly, and Hebrews turns the repetition itself into an argument. And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins (Hebrews 10:11). Every word in that sentence is doing work: the priest standeth, because there was no seat in the tabernacle — his work was never finished; he offers oftentimes the same sacrifices, and a remedy that must be endlessly repeated is thereby shown not to have cured anything. Two verses later comes the contrast: But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God. Luke uses the word of a demoniac’s long torment: for oftentimes it had caught him: and he was kept bound with chains and in fetters; and he brake the bands (Luke 8:29). Paul uses it of intentions repeatedly frustrated by providence: oftentimes I purposed to come unto you, (but was let hitherto,) that I might have some fruit among you also (Romans 1:13). And Ecclesiastes uses it to disarm a man offended by gossip: oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others (Ecclesiastes 7:22).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OFTENTIMES as frequently; often; many times; and notes the shorter form OFTTIMES with the same signification.
webster_full: OFTENTIMES, adv. — Frequently; often; many times; again and again.
OFTTIMES, adv. — The shorter form of the same word, also used in the Authorized Version.
OFTEN, adv. — Frequently; many times; not seldom.
Compounded of often and times, the plural adding emphasis to the repetition.
From Saxon oft, often — the root also of oftener and oftenest.
scriptures: Hebrews 10:11
And every priest standeth daily ministering and offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins:
Luke 8:29

(For he had commanded the unclean spirit to come out of the man. For oftentimes it had caught him: and he was kept bound with chains and in fetters; and he brake the bands, and was driven of the devil into the wilderness.)
Romans 1:13
Now I would not have you ignorant, brethren, that oftentimes I purposed to come unto you, (but was let hitherto,) that I might have some fruit among you also, even as among other Gentiles.
Ecclesiastes 7:22
For oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others.
corruption_summary: Hebrews 10:11 makes the repetition of a sacrifice the proof of its insufficiency, which is the New Testament’s own argument against the Roman doctrine of the Mass as a propitiatory offering repeated daily on thousands of altars.
corruption_paragraphs: The writer to the Hebrews builds his case on repetition. If the Levitical sacrifices had perfected the worshippers, would they not have ceased to be offered? (Hebrews 10:2). They did not cease; they were offered oftentimes, daily, standing; therefore they did not perfect anyone, and it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins. Against this stands the Roman doctrine, defined at Trent and reaffirmed since, that the Mass is a true and proper propitiatory sacrifice in which the same Christ is offered in an unbloody manner. Whatever the intention, the logic of Hebrews cuts straight through it: a sacrifice offered again is a sacrifice not finished. The contrast the chapter draws is between a priest who stands and a Priest who sat down, and the sitting is the whole argument.

Romans 1:13 offers a quieter correction. Paul purposed oftentimes to come to Rome and was hindered every time; he says so in the opening paragraph of the letter without a hint that the hindrance meant he had misread God’s will. He eventually reached Rome as a prisoner, after a shipwreck, at the empire’s expense. Repeated frustration of a good intention is not a verdict on the intention. Ecclesiastes 7:22 supplies a third and homelier use, and it is one of the wisest verses in Scripture for a wounded man: do not go looking for what people say of you, for oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others.
roots_summary: Greek pollakis (G4178), often, frequently; chronois pollois, for a long time; Hebrew peamim rabboth, many times; Greek ephapax (G2178), once for all — the deliberate contrast in Hebrews.
roots_lines: Greek pollakis (G4178) — often, many times; offering oftentimes the same sacrifices (Hebrews 10:11).
Greek ephapax (G2178) — once for all; the word Hebrews sets against pollakis (Hebrews 7:27, 9:12, 10:10).
Greek chronos (G5550) — time, duration; ofttimes it had caught him is pollois chronois in Luke 8:29.
Hebrew peamim (H6471) — times, occurrences; oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth (Ecclesiastes 7:22).
Greek kathemeran — daily; the priest of Hebrews 10:11 stands daily ministering.
usage: Offering oftentimes the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins (Hebrews 10:11) — repetition as proof of insufficiency.
Oftentimes I purposed to come unto you, (but was let hitherto,) (Romans 1:13) — repeated hindrance is not a verdict on the intention.
Thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others (Ecclesiastes 7:22) — the cure for listening at doors.

etymology: From speedy, from Saxon sped, success, haste. Webster 1828: quickly; with haste; in a short time. Scripture uses it in prayers for haste, in a warning about delayed justice, and in one of the Lord’s hardest sayings about His own delay.
biblical_def: Speedily in Scripture is asked for by men and promised by God, and the two do not always look the same from underneath. The psalmist asks for it plainly: Bow down thine ear to me; deliver me speedily: be thou my strong rock, for an house of defence to save me (Psalm 31:2), and again hide not thy face from thy servant; for I am in trouble: hear me speedily (Psalm 69:17). Ecclesiastes explains the moral consequence when justice is not speedy: Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil (Ecclesiastes 8:11). Delay does not merely postpone a penalty; it emboldens, and the Preacher names that as the mechanism by which societies grow bold in wickedness. The hardest use is the Lord’s own, at the end of the parable of the importunate widow and the unjust judge: I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth? (Luke 18:8). The promise of speed and the question about surviving faith stand in the same verse, which is the honest shape of the matter.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SPEEDILY as quickly; with haste; in a short time; without delay.
webster_full: SPEEDILY, adv. — Quickly; with haste; in a short time; soon.
SPEEDY, a. Quick; swift; nimble; hasty; rapid in motion or performance.
Applied to the execution of justice, to deliverance, and to the answering of prayer.
SPEED, n. — In its old sense, success or good fortune, as in the phrase to send one good speed.
From Saxon sped, success, haste — the root also of speed, godspeed, and expedite.
scriptures: Psalm 31:2
Bow down thine ear to me; deliver me speedily: be thou my strong rock, for an house of defence to save me.
Psalm 69:17
And hide not thy face from thy servant; for I am in trouble: hear me speedily.
Ecclesiastes 8:11
Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
Luke 18:8
I tell you that he will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?
corruption_summary: Luke 18:8 promises that God will avenge His elect speedily and then asks whether faith will be found on the earth at His coming, and any reading that keeps only one half of the verse misrepresents what the Lord said.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable is about a widow and a judge who feared not God, neither regarded man, and who granted her plea only because her persistence wearied him. The Lord’s argument is from the lesser to the greater: if an unjust judge yields to importunity, shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him, though he bear long with them? The though he bear long is in the promise. Then: he will avenge them speedily — and immediately, Nevertheless when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth? The speed is measured from God’s side and the crying is day and night from ours, and the Lord evidently anticipated that the interval would exhaust many. Preaching that promises quick answers has removed the nevertheless; preaching that never promises vindication at all has removed the speedily.

Ecclesiastes 8:11 deserves separate attention because it explains something about societies as well as souls. Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil. Delay in justice does not leave the wicked where they were; it hardens them, because they draw the conclusion that nothing follows wrongdoing. This is an argument for the diligent and prompt punishment of crime by the magistrate, whom Romans 13:4 calls a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. It is also, read the other way, a description of the danger every believer is in during a season when God is patient with him and nothing appears to happen.
roots_summary: Hebrew meherah (H4120), speedily, quickly; mahar (H4116), to hasten; Greek en tachei (G5034), in speed, shortly; tachus (G5036), quick.
roots_lines: Hebrew meherah (H4120) — speed, haste; deliver me speedily (Psalm 31:2).
Hebrew mahar (H4116) — to hasten, to make haste; the verb behind the adverb.
Hebrew pithgam (H6599) — a decree, a sentence; sentence against an evil work (Ecclesiastes 8:11).
Greek en tachei (G5034) — in quickness, speedily; he will avenge them speedily (Luke 18:8).
Greek ekdikeo (G1556) — to avenge, to vindicate; the verb of the widow’s plea and of God’s answer.
usage: Deliver me speedily (Psalm 31:2) — the prayer, asked plainly.
Because sentence… is not executed speedily (Ecclesiastes 8:11) — delay does not postpone evil, it emboldens it.
He will avenge them speedily. Nevertheless… shall he find faith on the earth? (Luke 18:8) — both halves, in one verse.

etymology: From short, Saxon sceort, and the adverbial -ly. Webster 1828: quickly; soon; in a little time; also, briefly, in few words. Revelation opens with it, and how it is understood governs how the whole book is read.
biblical_def: Shortly in the New Testament is a word of imminence, and it appears at three very different scales. Of ordinary Christian travel: I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face (3 John 1:14) — a letter cut short because the writer expects to arrive. Of a man’s own approaching death, spoken with striking calm: Knowing that shortly I must put off this my tabernacle, even as our Lord Jesus Christ hath shewed me (2 Peter 1:14). Of the promised crushing of the enemy: And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly (Romans 16:20) — the language of Genesis 3:15, and the bruising is under your feet, the church sharing the victory of its Head. And of the whole book of Revelation: The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass (Revelation 1:1), repeated at the book’s close in Revelation 22:6. What John was shown was given to servants as things that must shortly come to pass, and the book ends Surely I come quickly.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SHORTLY as quickly; soon; in a little time; and, in a second sense, briefly or in few words.
webster_full: SHORTLY, adv. — Quickly; soon; in a little time; before long.
In few words; briefly; as, to state a matter shortly.
SHORT, a. — Not long; not extended in time or space; brief.
Applied in Scripture both to a near event and to the whole span of the present age as God measures it.
From Saxon sceort, short — the root also of shorten, shortage, and shirt.
scriptures: Revelation 1:1
The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:
Romans 16:20
And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you. Amen.
2 Peter 1:14
Knowing that shortly I must put off this my tabernacle, even as our Lord Jesus Christ hath shewed me.
3 John 1:14
But I trust I shall shortly see thee, and we shall speak face to face. Peace be to thee. Our friends salute thee. Greet the friends by name.
corruption_summary: Full preterism takes shortly in Revelation 1:1 to mean that every prophecy in the book was fulfilled by AD 70, which requires the resurrection and the second coming to be past events and is therefore outside the bounds of orthodoxy.
corruption_paragraphs: The word does real work and cannot simply be spiritualised away; partial preterism, which reads much of Matthew 24 and parts of Revelation as fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem, is within Reformed orthodoxy and the dictionary treats it as such. What is not within orthodoxy is the full-preterist claim that all prophecy was fulfilled in AD 70, including the resurrection of the body and the second coming. Paul names that error by its first-century form: Hymenaeus and Philetus, who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:18). Every creed the church has confessed looks forward to a bodily return and a bodily resurrection, and 1 Corinthians 15 makes the future resurrection of believers inseparable from the past resurrection of Christ.

The opposite error treats shortly and quickly as meaning nothing at all, so that the church settles into an indefinite present with no expectation. That is the mockery Peter answers — Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were — and his reply is not that the promise was figurative but that God measures time differently and is being patient. Romans 16:20 shows the pastoral use of the word: Paul tells a divided, harassed church that the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly, and it is offered as comfort in the middle of a warning about those who cause divisions. The nearness is meant to be felt.
roots_summary: Greek en tachei (G5034), in speed, shortly; tachu (G5035), quickly; tacheos (G5030), soon; syntemno (G4932), to cut short.
roots_lines: Greek en tachei (G5034) — with speed, shortly; things which must shortly come to pass (Revelation 1:1).
Greek tachu (G5035) — quickly; Surely I come quickly (Revelation 22:20).
Greek tacheos (G5030) — soon, hastily; shortly I must put off this my tabernacle (2 Peter 1:14).
Greek skenoma (G4638) — a tent, a tabernacle; Peter’s word for his own body.
Greek suntribo (G4937) — to crush, to break in pieces; shall bruise Satan under your feet (Romans 16:20).
usage: Things which must shortly come to pass (Revelation 1:1) — the word that governs how the book is read.
The God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly (Romans 16:20) — Genesis 3:15, and under the church’s feet.
Shortly I must put off this my tabernacle (2 Peter 1:14) — a man naming his own death with calm.

etymology: From Saxon aet foran, at the front — the older form of before. Webster 1828: before; sooner in time; in front. Retained in the Authorized Version and in the compounds aforetime, aforehand, and aforesaid.
biblical_def: Afore is the older form of before, and in Paul’s hands it does theological work at the very front of Romans. The gospel he preaches is not a novelty: Which he had promised afore by his prophets in the holy scriptures (Romans 1:2) — the second verse of the epistle, establishing that the gospel of God concerning His Son was announced in advance, in writing, by named prophets. Paul uses it again for the eternal purpose behind salvation: that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory (Romans 9:23), where the preparation of the vessels of mercy precedes their existence and stands in deliberate contrast to the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction in the previous verse. He uses it of his own earlier writing: as I wrote afore in few words (Ephesians 3:3). And Isaiah uses it in a vinedresser’s figure for judgment falling before the fruit is gathered: For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks (Isaiah 18:5).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines AFORE as before; sooner in time; in front of; and notes that it is now nearly superseded by before, except in composition and in the Scriptures.
webster_full: AFORE, adv. — Before; sooner in time; previously.
AFORE, prep. — In front of; in the presence of; prior to.
Now chiefly retained in composition — aforetime, aforehand, aforesaid, aforementioned.
In the Authorized Version, used interchangeably with before, and preserved for its brevity in verse.
From Saxon aet foran, at the front; compare the German vor and the English fore.
scriptures: Romans 1:2
(Which he had promised afore by his prophets in the holy scriptures,)
Romans 9:23
And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory,
Ephesians 3:3
How that by revelation he made known unto me the mystery; (as I wrote afore in few words,
Isaiah 18:5
For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the sour grape is ripening in the flower, he shall both cut off the sprigs with pruning hooks, and take away and cut down the branches.
corruption_summary: Romans 1:2 stakes the gospel’s credibility on its having been promised in advance in the Hebrew scriptures, which forecloses every reconstruction of Christianity as a religion that emerged from its environment rather than being announced beforehand.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul puts it in the second verse of Romans and never argues for it afterwards, because the whole epistle assumes it: the gospel of God which he had promised afore by his prophets in the holy scriptures. Peter says the same at Pentecost, Philip preached Christ to the eunuch out of Isaiah 53, and the risen Lord Himself began at Moses and all the prophets. Against this, the history-of-religions approach explains the New Testament as a first-century synthesis of Jewish apocalyptic and Hellenistic mystery religion, and its modern popular form treats Christian doctrine as a set of later developments read back into the text. But the promise is in writing, in a book the church’s opponents also possessed and could check, which is exactly why Paul appealed to it in synagogues rather than around them.

Romans 9:23 sets the word inside the hardest chapter in Paul, and the dictionary states the doctrine plainly. The vessels of mercy are those God had afore prepared unto glory — prepared beforehand, by Him, and not on the basis of anything foreseen in them, since verse 11 has already said the choice was made the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil. Note also the deliberate asymmetry in the grammar that Paul chose: the vessels of wrath are fitted to destruction, with no agent named, while God is explicitly the one who afore prepared the vessels of mercy. Election and reprobation are not mirror images, and Reformed theology has always been careful at exactly this point.
roots_summary: Greek proepaggellomai (G4279), to promise beforehand; proetoimazo (G4282), to prepare beforehand; prographo (G4270), to write before; Hebrew liphne, before, in front of.
roots_lines: Greek proepaggellomai (G4279) — to promise beforehand; promised afore by his prophets (Romans 1:2).
Greek proetoimazo (G4282) — to make ready beforehand; afore prepared unto glory (Romans 9:23), and used of the good works of Ephesians 2:10.
Greek prographo (G4270) — to write before; as I wrote afore in few words (Ephesians 3:3).
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to fit, to complete; the fitted to destruction of Romans 9:22, notably without a named agent.
Hebrew liphne — before the face of, in front of; the ordinary Hebrew expression of priority in time and place.
usage: Promised afore by his prophets in the holy scriptures (Romans 1:2) — the gospel announced in advance, in writing.
Vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory (Romans 9:23) — prepared beforehand, and by God.
Afore the harvest… he shall both cut off the sprigs (Isaiah 18:5) — judgment falling before the fruit is gathered.
